list.listitem: Diabetic peripheral neuropathy (DPN) is an important risk factor for gait disturbance, falls, foot ulcers, infection, and subsequent amputations. C
Control glucose to prevent the development of DPN. A
Patients with diabetes should be screened for DPN at the time of diagnosis and annually using simple diagnostic tests. C
Clinicians should educate all patients with DPN in general foot care, including regular inspection of their feet and proper footwear. B
Treat DPN using oral amitriptylene, duloxetine, or a gabapentinoid (eg, gabapentin or pregabalin), either as monotherapy or combined therapy. A
Topical capsaicin may be an effective treatment for DPN. B

background.definition: Nerve damage is the most common complication of type 1 and type 2 diabetes mellitus (DM). The most frequent neuropathy is symmetric distal polyneuropathy (SDPN). SDPN can produce paresthesia, pain, loss of sensation, or weakness (typically in the feet and lower extremities). Sensorimotor neuropathy of SDPN can lead to foot ulcers and amputation. Other patterns of nerve damage in diabetes include those affecting a single cranial or peripheral nerve (mononeuropathy), multiple peripheral nerves (mononeuropathy multiplex), nerve roots (radiculopathies), and the autonomic nervous system. Autonomic neuropathies include cardiac autonomic neuropathy, angina, orthostatic hypotension, gastroparesis, genitourinary neuropathy, loss of sensation of hypoglycemia, and other symptoms. This chapter will not discuss these syndromes.

list.listitem: The annual incidence of DPN in patients with type 1 DM (T1DM) is approximately 20 per 1000 person-years and 61 per 1000 person-years in patients with type 2 DM (T2DM).
10%-30% of patients with prediabetes or metabolic syndrome can develop DPN, particularly painful neuropathy.
At the time of diagnosis, 10%-30% of patients with diabetes have DPN.
T1DM: 280 per 1000 persons.
T2DM: Prevalence increases with time from 83 per 1000 at the time of diagnosis to 420 per 1000 ten years or more after diagnosis.
Painful DPN occurs in nearly 35% of patients with DM and is more common in T2DM, women, and South Asians.

In a retrospective study, 11% or more patients with DM are at risk for lower extremity amputation. Compared to patients without DM, patients with DM were 400 times more likely to undergo toe amputations and 12 times more likely to have a below-knee amputation.
The development of symptomatic DPN affects the quality of life and is the strongest single predictor of depressive and other mental symptoms among persons with diabetes.
Sustained hyperglycemia is the most critical risk factor in developing diabetic neuropathy.
Comorbid problems: Incidence of neuropathy is also associated with elevated triglyceride levels, high body mass index (BMI), smoking, and hypertension.
Nerve damage in diabetes is most likely multifactorial, including hyperglycemia, direct metabolic effects from advanced glycation end products, sorbitol, and oxidative injury.
Ischemia and hemodynamic changes due to microvascular disease have also been implicated.

A case report of patients treated with insulin, causing rapid improvement in glycemic control, complicated by severe sensory insulin neuritis, showed abnormal nutrient blood vessels around the nerves and proliferation of new blood vessels similar to those found in patients with proliferative retinopathy.
Painful DPN is more common in female patients and patients with small fiber dysfunction.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Height, espeically if taller than 175.5 cm (5 ft, 9 in).

list.listitem: Patients with diabetes should be screened for peripheral neuropathy at the time of diagnosis and annually after that. C
Optimizing blood sugar control in patients with T1DM and T2DM can prevent or postpone the likelihood of developing DPN but carries other risks. A
Patients with prediabetes or metabolic syndrome may have DPN. Consider screening in this population.
Up to 50% of patients with DPN are asymptomatic.
DPN is a significant risk factor for lower extremity amputation among patients with diabetes.

The American Association of Clinical Endocrinologists recommends screening for autonomic neuropathy and DPN in all patients with T1DM five years after diagnosis, at the time of diagnosis for patients with T2DM, and annually after that.
The American Diabetes Association (ADA) recommends that all patients with DM should be screened for DPN at the time of diagnosis and at least annually using simple clinical tests.
Prevention is the cornerstone of care for DPN.

In patients with T2DM with no clinical evidence of DPN, skin biopsy showed a decline in the intraepidermal nerve fiber density (IENFD). Regular individualized weekly supervised exercise of 60-90 minutes or more, in addition to home exercise, have been shown to increase the IENFD.
All patients with DM should be educated in general foot care, including regular inspection of the feet and proper footwear. B

For patients with T1DM, intensive therapy reduced the incidence of confirmed clinical neuropathy after five years of follow-up in the Diabetes Control and Complications Trial (DCCT); the absolute risk reduction was 7% in patients with no retinopathy at baseline (NNT = 14) and 9% in those with baseline retinopathy (NNT = 11).

The Action to Control Cardiovascular Disease in Diabetes (ACCORD) showed in patients with T2DM, intensive therapy postponed the onset of DPN (NNT = 33) but did not decrease the risk of advanced complications.

Intensive therapy aims to decrease HbA1C to less than 6%, was associated with severe hypoglycemia, weight gain, and cardiovascular-related mortality. Intensive treatment should be used with extreme caution.
To reduce their risk of DPN, patients who smoke should be counseled to quit.

Patients are at high risk for lower extremities ulcer or amputation if they have a history of ulcer or amputation, foot deformity, abnormal monofilament testing, visual impairment, poor blood glucose control, diabetic nephropathy, or smoking.

In a high-risk population, a systematic approach to foot examination for patients with diabetes, including sensory screening in asymptomatic patients, reduced the incidence of lower extremity amputation by 48% compared with usual care.
Simple diagnostic tests such as monofilament testing, on-off vibration with the 128-MHz tuning fork, or superficial pain sensation are sufficient to detect and diagnose DPN. B
Before making the diagnosis of DPN, one must exclude other causes (see differential diagnosis). C

list.listitem: Patients with diabetes should be asked regularly about the presence of typical symptoms, including a symmetric loss of sensation or complaint of numbness in the distal lower extremities. Other symptoms can include burning, painful sensations, or weakness in the ankle or foot.
Atypical DPN symptoms are rapid onset, asymmetrical distribution, and motor involvement greater than sensory involvement.
Simple clinical tests, performed annually, as listed below, are sufficient for diagnosis unless clinical features are atypical.

Testing methods, including monofilament testing, on-off vibration with a 128-MHZ tuning fork, duration of vibratory sensation, and superficial pain sensation, produce comparable results and are all helpful screening tests in patients with diabetes.
Inter-rater reliability is acceptable with ankle reflex, four-site monofilament, and vibration perception threshold.
The ADA recommends assessment of ankle reflexes and testing vibration perception threshold with a biothesiometer to detect loss of protective sensation.

Each test has relatively low sensitivity (22%-41%). Performing combinations of tests increase sensitivity to 87% in detecting DPN (but reduces specificity). Therefore, the ADA suggests using the monofilament with 1 of the five additional tests.
Electrophysiologic or quantitative sensory testing is rarely needed in the presence of symptoms or documented loss of sensation, except in situations where clinical features are atypical.
Electrophysiologic or quantitative sensory testing may help document changes in sensory thresholds in the longitudinal evaluation of patients with DPN.

There is no prospective evidence that patients with abnormalities on quantitative sensory testing who lack clinical evidence of DPN will ultimately go on to develop clinical neuropathy. Quantitative sensory testing should, therefore, not be used to detect preclinical neuropathy.
Consider referring to a neurologist when the patient's symptoms are atypical and the diagnosis is unclear.
Reqularly ask about symptoms of DPN.
Screen annually in high-risk patients using one of the following methods:
If abnormal, ask about motor or autonomic neuropathy sympotms and rule out other causes (see Differential Diagnosis).
Identify and optimize risk factors that can worsen DPN, such as hypertension, smoking, obesity, and hypertriglyceridemia.
Electrodiagnostic testing may be helpful if the diagnosis remains uncertain due to atypical features.
Treat DPN using oral amitriptylene, duloxetine, or a gabapentinoid (eg, gabapentin or pregabalin), either as monotherapy or combined therapy. A
Topical capsaicin may be an effective treatment for DPN. B
Duloxetine, at dosages of 60 to 120 mg daily, has shown modest benefit for treating painful diabetic neuropathy.

Most RCTs on SNRIs and neuropathic pain used duloxetine. A systematic review concluded that venlafaxine was also effective, but a Cochrane review found no convincing evidence for its efficacy and therefore did not recommend its routine use.
In general, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) are not effective for treating DPN.

A meta-analysis showed neuropathic pain had a clinically significant response to anticonvalsants, with the NNT = 7. There was no difference in the efficacy between gabapentin, oxcarbazepine, pregabalin, or topiramate., Pregabalin was shown in one RCT to decrease pain scores and is also FDA-approved for treating painful diabetic neuropathy.

Gabapentin at 1200 mg to 3600 mg daily dose was found to be effective in a Cochrane review, based on moderate quality evidence. Out of 10 patients taking gabapentin, 3 to 4 will experience 50% pain reduction compared to 1 to 2 for placebo, but more than half will not achieve this pain reduction and may experience adverse events.

Pregabalin 300mg daily dose appears effective for DPN, based on a Cochrane review. About a third of patients will experience 50% pain reduction, nearly half will experience 30% pain reduction, but more than half will not achieve meaninful pain reduction and may experience adverse events (eg, somnolence).
Valproate 500 mg twice daily may be effective in reducing pain from DPN.
Carbamazepine 400 mg twice daily may also be effective in treating chronic pain.

Tricyclic antidepressants (eg, amitriptyline 25-100 mg at bedtime, nortriptyline 25-75 mg at bedtime, or imipramine 25-75 mg at bedtime) have been used historically to treat DPN. However, a Cochrane review did not find evidence for the efficacy of imipramine.

Based on a Cochrane review of 17 RCTs involving 1342 patients, amitriptylene's effectiveness is not supported by moderate or high certainty evidence, but the authors admit amitriptylene has been used successfully for decades to treat DPN. The authors also found no evidence proving its lack of efficacy and they go on to recommend its continued use while acknowledging only a minority of patients will experience satisfactory pain relief from it.

A crossover RCT of 130 adults with painful diabetic neuropathy for at least 3 months found similar proportions of responders to amitriptyline (37%), duloxetine (32%), and pregabalin (34%), and higher response rates (40-50%) for two-drug combinations.

A comprehensive systematic review identified 57 relevant studies. It concluded that there is adequate evidence that duloxetine, venlafaxine, pregabalin, oxcarbazepine, tricyclics, atypical opioids, and botulinum toxin are all more effective than placebo at reducing pain. The evidence was critiqued for often not including quality of life measures, and for the short duration of studies.

Cochrane reviews failed to find convincing evidence for the efficacy of tramadol, morphine, and oxycodone to treat DPN. Considering the adverse events associated with their chronic use, they are not recommended for routine treatment of DPN.
Topical capsaicin 0.075% applied four times daily to the feet effectively reduced pain in a meta-analysis of 4 pooled trialsand a Cochrane review.
Topical clonidine may be effective for DPN but this is based on low to very low certainty evidence, according to a Cochrane review of 4 RCTs.
Topical 5% lidocaine patches were used in open-label, nonrandomized trials; there are insufficient data to recommend their use.

Intensive insulin therapy was associated with improvements in nerve conduction on electrophysiologic testing, but this has not been shown to improve DPN symptoms that are already present (eg, loss of sensation or pain syndromes). Intensive therapy may carry risks in patients with T2DM and microalbuminuria at high risk of DPN.
Based on separate Cochrane reviews, there is insufficient evidence for acetyl-L-carnitive, while alpha-lipoic acid may have little to no effect for DPN.

Although some have advocated surgical decompression for medial and lateral plantar tunnel syndromes, there is insufficient evidence at this time to support the routine use of surgical decompression. A Cochrane systematic review found no prospective clinical trials.
Vitamin E is not more effective than placebo.
There is insufficient evidence currently to support botanicals or nutritional interventions.
A Cochrane review found insufficient evidence for the effectiveness of nutmeg or St. John's wort for DPN.
A systematic review of 11 RCTs (N=927) with mostly disease-oriented outcomes suggested that moxibustion may be helpful for some patients with DPN.

A systematic review of 41 randomized controlled trials (RCTs) exploring the potential therapeutic benefit of exercise and neuropathy showed a benefit when patients with neuropathy exercise. Combining endurance and sensorimotor training is the most beneficial exercise for patients with DPN.
Sensorimotor training is any exercise involving the engagement of both the sensory and motor functions to enhance balance and motor control.
The pressure against the feet during the day is not present at night, and the symptoms may worsen. Wearing socks while sleeping may help mild symptoms.
All patients should be educated about foot care, including regular inspection and proper footwear.
Therapeutic shoes or customized inserts are not recommended for routine use in patients with DPN.
In a small trial, patients treated with TENS units showed significant lower pain scores than those with sham cutaneous stimulation.
Patients should be taught general foot care and the importance of daily foot inspection for ulceration.

A multidisciplinary approach is recommended for patients who develop foot ulcers or have undergone prior amputations, including possible podiatric evaluation and surveillance and circulation evaluation by ankle-brachial index measurement.
Patients with DPN, documented by insensitivity to monofilament, have twice the risk of diabetic foot ulcerations. B
The best predictors of foot ulcer at a 3-year follow-up are impaired vision, prior foot ulcer, tinea pedis, onychomycosis, monofilament insensitivity, and increased hemoglobin A1C. B
The length of time and severity of hyperglycemia, as measured by hemoglobin A1C, is predictive of DPN.
Up to 47% of patients with diabetes eventually develop DPN.

The risk of ulcers and amputation increased in people with poor glycemic control, DPN, foot deformity, a past history of foot ulcer, peripheral vascular disease, previous amputation, vision impairment, diabetic nephropathy, and cigarette smoking.

In the Seattle Diabetic Foot study, the foot ulcer incidence at follow-up was 5 per 100 person-years after three years. The best predictors included hemoglobin A1C, monofilament insensitivity, tinea pedis, onychomycosis, prior foot ulcer, and impaired vision.
Persons with insensitivity to monofilament have double the risk of developing foot ulceration.

In the DCCT trial of patients with T1DM, at 5-year follow-up, 3% of patients in the no baseline retinopathy and 7% of those in the mild baseline retinopathy group on intensive therapy had developed neuropathy compared with 10% and 16% of patients without and with retinopathy in the control group.

Patients should be educated about their risk factors for foot ulcers and encouraged to perform good foot and nail care and daily foot monitoring; if unable to do this, clinicians can instruct a family member to monitor them.
Patients with foot or ankle deformities may need extra-wide or deep shoes or custom-molded shoes for foot protection and comfort.
